meaning: The difference between what a simulator produces and what the real robot and bench produce, in physics, appearance and timing.
Carrying a policy trained in simulation onto the real robot.
Carrying something real into the simulator: measured servo parameters, a scanned scene, or a policy trained on real data to be tested there.
Drawing each uncertain simulator parameter from a range at the start of every episode, so the real world falls inside what the policy trained on.
Fitting a simulator's parameters to recordings of the real robot until the simulated motion matches the measured one.
The system-identification toolbox that ships with MuJoCo 4.0; the SO-101 script built on it fits 24 servo parameters from one episode.
The step that tells the software what each joint's encoder reading means as an angle; done by hand on this arm, it can leave the gripper 10 to 20 mm or more off.
The tool at the end of the arm, here the gripper.
Deployed on the real robot with no further training on real data.
A control rule that pushes in proportion to the position error and brakes in proportion to the speed.
How hard a servo pushes per unit of position error.
How hard a servo or joint brakes per unit of speed.
Extra inertia at a joint from the spinning motor and its gears.
A constant resistance inside a joint that the motor must overcome before the joint moves.
A fitting method for sums of squared misses: work out how each miss changes with each parameter, then step all parameters at once to where the squared misses would be smallest.
The time a command takes to travel over the serial link to the servos.
Representing a filmed place as a cloud of small, soft, coloured blobs fitted until pictures drawn from the cloud match the video frames.
A simulated copy of a real place built from a video: splats for how it looks and a mesh for what objects collide with.
GPU units that accelerate ray tracing, covered in section 13; Isaac Sim's RTX renderer needs them and the A100 and H100 lack them.
The physics engine of NVIDIA's Isaac Sim; under it, physics parameters are changed through the CPU.
One teleoperated recording driven so that every fitted constant acts in the data: small corrections, fast motion, starts and stops, and moves from rest on every joint.
Google DeepMind's suite of robot tasks built on MuJoCo; it ships the SO-101 pick-cube task and the system-identification script.
The Playground task that trains an SO-101 vision policy in simulation to pick a cube up and deploys it zero-shot.
The largest torque the simulated servo may apply, 2.94 N m, set from the 12 V servo's stall torque and not fitted.
The torque a motor produces when held still at full power; the servo datasheet's figure for its strength.
An offset the task adds to the simulated joint readings each episode, to stand in for calibration error.
A 2024 suite for scoring real-robot policies in simulation.
NVIDIA's robot-learning framework on top of Isaac Sim.
NVIDIA's robot simulator, rendering through Omniverse RTX.
A 2024 method in which a language model writes the reward and proposes domain-randomisation ranges.
An actuator model that is a neural network trained on hardware data, used in Isaac Lab in place of an ideal PD loop.
A research pipeline that builds scanned scenes from a short video and tests policies in them.
In PolaRiS, fine-tuning a policy briefly on simulated demonstrations from other scanned scenes so it is used to the simulator's rendering.
A measure from -1 to 1 of how closely two sets of scores rise and fall together.
The GPU version of MuJoCo; its batch renderer can ray trace splat files without RTX hardware.
The geometry type Isaac Sim's scene files use to store Gaussian splats.
NVIDIA's splat reconstruction code, with a ray-traced method (3DGRT) and a rasterised one (3DGUT).
Another robot project whose motor parameters the SO-101 maker's model file adapts.
